clue.text: Poisonous growth on musical authority created by J. B. Priestley

definitions.note: the definition names the play by what made it, a Priestley comedy of 1933

parts.note: the laburnum is a tree whose seeds and pods are toxic
Grove's Dictionary of Music and Musicians is the standard reference work on music

explanation.surface: A toxic plant sits on top of a music textbook, something the playwright Priestley dreamt up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' puts the tree before the music dictionary in this down-the-page style charade; the definition points to Priestley's suburban comedy set in a London street.
explanation.definitionFit: Priestley wrote a 1933 stage comedy with this title, about a respectable suburban man secretly a counterfeiter.

clue.text: Her lover knew her husband's game

definitions.text: Her lover knew her husband's game

parts.words: Her lover knew her husband's game
parts.note: the lover is a gamekeeper on the husband's estate, so he literally knows the husband's game birds, not his tricks

explanation.surface: A wife's lover has seen through the husband's scheming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' reads as a scheme, but in Lawrence's novel the heroine's lover Mellors is the gamekeeper who looks after her husband Sir Clifford's pheasants.
explanation.definitionFit: D. H. Lawrence's heroine, wife of Sir Clifford, takes the estate gamekeeper Mellors as her lover.

clue.text: Betjeman's were expected to pay a friendly visit to Berkshire

definitions.text: Betjeman's were expected to pay a friendly visit to Berkshire

parts.words: Betjeman's were expected to pay a friendly visit to Berkshire
parts.note: Betjeman's poem about Slough opens by inviting friendly explosives to fall on the town, now in Berkshire

explanation.surface: Something the poet Betjeman hoped would call amicably on an English county.
explanation.walkthrough: John Betjeman's poem 'Slough' begins 'Come friendly bombs and fall on Slough'; Slough, a town west of London, has been in the county of Berkshire since 1974.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet asks for explosive devices dropped from aircraft to land on Slough, calling them 'friendly'.

clue.text: Losing ground, like Malvolio? (gartered, or otherwise)

indicators.note: otherwise asks for the letters of gartered and or to be set out in another way

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Malvolio, wearing his cross-garters, is in decline, or perhaps not.
explanation.walkthrough: In Twelfth Night Malvolio is tricked into appearing cross-gartered, which explains 'like Malvolio?' as a nod to the fodder word 'gartered'; 'otherwise' rearranges GARTERED OR.
explanation.definitionFit: Something going backwards or deteriorating is losing ground, the sense of moving back rather than forward.

clue.text: I use Lit, perhaps, literally to define use

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters of I use Lit may be some other word once rearranged

explanation.surface: A dictionary note telling how the abbreviation 'Lit' is employed to explain a word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges the seven letters of I USE LIT; 'literally to define' tells the solver the answer is a word defined as 'use'.
explanation.definitionFit: To employ something is to make use of it, the verb form of putting to service.

clue.text: Her work was right at last

definitions.text: Her work was right at last

parts.words: Her work was right at last
parts.note: one of this Victorian novelist's stories, collected in 1860, is titled Right at Last

explanation.surface: A woman's job turned out well in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The words read as praise for someone's effort, but 'Right at Last' is the title of a short story, and of an 1860 collection, by the Victorian novelist Elizabeth Gaskell.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of Cranford published a tale called Right at Last, first printed in Household Words.

clue.text: Alternatively very loud composer

parts.note: alternatively means or
ff, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: A choice between options, or perhaps a deafening musician.
explanation.definitionFit: Carl Orff was the German composer of Carmina Burana.

clue.text: Interpreter gives former example and French first

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
eg is the abbreviation for for example
et is French for and
1st, with the figure read as the letter I, gives IST

explanation.surface: A translator offers an old instance and some French to begin with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and French' reads as a list item, but 'French' and 'and' together give ET, the French word for 'and'; '1st' is written with I for the numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: An exegetist explains texts, especially scripture, so is an interpreter of them.

clue.text: Bitter Rice

parts.note: names an Italian film, but read as a description of a sour man called Rice, the music-hall comic Archie Rice

explanation.surface: The title of a classic Italian neorealist film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bitter Rice' is a 1949 Italian film, but here it describes Archie Rice, the embittered, failing music-hall comic at the centre of John Osborne's 1957 play.
explanation.definitionFit: Osborne's play centres on Archie Rice, a cynical and resentful variety performer.

clue.text: Writer on style emits rude version

indicators.note: a version of emits rude is the same letters given a new form

explanation.surface: An author on prose style puts out a coarse draft.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek treatise On Style is attributed to Demetrius, so he is an ancient writer about style.

clue.text: By forms unfashioned, — from Nature's hand " (O. Goldsmith)

definitions.text: By forms unfashioned, — from Nature's hand " (O. Goldsmith)

parts.words: By forms unfashioned, — from Nature's hand " (O. Goldsmith)
parts.note: a line from Goldsmith's poem The Traveller with one word missing, the word meaning new or untouched

explanation.surface: A quotation from Oliver Goldsmith with a word blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: The line in Goldsmith's The Traveller reads 'By forms unfashion'd, fresh from Nature's hand'; the missing word fills the dash.
explanation.definitionFit: Something new and untouched, straight from nature, is described with this adjective in the quoted line.

clue.text: Kid fathered by O. Henry

parts.note: a child born to a man called Henry, but really a fictional bandit created by the writer O. Henry

explanation.surface: A child whose father was a man named Henry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kid' is a child, but the Cisco Kid is the outlaw hero of O. Henry's 1907 story 'The Caballero's Way'; 'fathered' means created.
explanation.definitionFit: The writer O. Henry invented the Cisco Kid, a Western character later famous on film and radio.

clue.text: Byron's prudish mother

parts.note: not the poet's own mother but Donna ..., the strait-laced mother of Don Juan in Byron's poem

explanation.surface: The poet Byron had a straitlaced mother.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue seems to be about Byron's real mother, but means the mother he created for Don Juan: Donna Inez, a learned and prim woman.
explanation.definitionFit: In Byron's Don Juan the hero's mother, Donna Inez, is satirised as rigidly moral and pedantic.

clue.text: Barbara Pym's suitably venerable spinster sisters

definitions.text: Barbara Pym's suitably venerable spinster sisters

parts.words: Barbara Pym's suitably venerable spinster sisters
parts.note: the unmarried sisters Belinda and Harriet in Pym's novel Some Tame Gazelle share a surname with the Venerable monk-historian

explanation.surface: Two elderly unmarried sisters in a Barbara Pym novel are fittingly respected.
explanation.walkthrough: In Some Tame Gazelle Pym's spinsters are Belinda and Harriet Bede; 'suitably venerable' alludes to the Venerable Bede, the Anglo-Saxon monk and historian.
explanation.definitionFit: Pym gave her two middle-aged sisters the surname of the early English church historian known as the Venerable.

clue.text: My apparent claim to be a journalist, I have to add, is awesome

parts.words: My apparent claim to be a journalist
parts.note: a journalist might say 'I am press', shortened to I'm press
I have contracts to I've

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of being a reporter and adds that he finds it all inspiring.
explanation.walkthrough: A journalist's claim reads 'I'm press'; 'to add' attaches I'VE to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that inspires awe is grand and striking, the sense of making a strong impression.

clue.text: Rue meal prepared for son of Duke of York

indicators.note: prepared suggests the letters of rue meal are cooked up into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A dish of rue is cooked up for a young aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Richard II, Aumerle is the son of the Duke of York.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Richard II has Aumerle as the son of Edmund, Duke of York, who plots against Bolingbroke.

clue.text: Chap's area represented by woman writer

parts.note: a chap is a man, so chap's is man's
a field is an area, as in a field of study

explanation.surface: A man's patch of land stands for a female author.
explanation.definitionFit: Katherine Mansfield was a New Zealand-born short-story writer.

clue.text: The French graduate is on time, like a monk

parts.note: la is a French word for the
an MA, Master of Arts, is a graduate

explanation.surface: A French graduate turns up punctually and lives like a monk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is on time' reads as punctual, but supplies IS then T; the answer describes a Tibetan Buddhist lama.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamaism is Tibetan Buddhism, whose priests and monks are lamas, so the adjective applies to a monk there.

clue.text: Surprisingly denotes scene of Roman naval victory in 86BC

definitions.text: scene of Roman naval victory in 86BC

indicators.note: surprisingly indicates the letters of denotes fall into an unexpected order

explanation.surface: A word unexpectedly names the site of an ancient Roman sea battle.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenedos, an Aegean island near Troy, was where Lucullus defeated a Pontic fleet during the Mithridatic War.

clue.text: Somehow spice in ship gives rise to philosophical doubt

indicators.note: in places the shuffled spice inside the letters for the ship

parts.note: SS, steamship, is the standard abbreviation for a ship

indicators.note: somehow says the letters of spice come out in some different order

explanation.surface: Spice stowed on board a vessel leads someone to start questioning everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gives rise to' is only a link; the shuffled spice is carried aboard the ship, and the answer is a rare Greek-derived word for doubt.
explanation.definitionFit: Scepsis is the sceptical attitude, the Greek-derived word for philosophical questioning.

clue.text: 16 said that he never got any further than warming the teapot

definitions.text: 16 said that he never got any further than warming the teapot

parts.words: 16 said that he never got any further than warming the teapot
parts.note: the woman writer of 16 down, Katherine Mansfield, made this jibe about a fellow novelist

explanation.surface: A writer is mocked for never getting past the first step of making tea.
explanation.walkthrough: Katherine Mansfield (16 down) wrote of E. M. Forster that he 'never gets any further than warming the teapot': all preparation, no tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Mansfield's remark was aimed at the author of A Passage to India and Howards End.

clue.text: Sudden emphases of South Africa in loud passages

indicators.note: in puts the South African code inside the musical plural

parts.note: forti is the plural of forte, a loud passage in music
ZA is the international code for South Africa

explanation.surface: Bursts of stress in a South African score's noisy sections.
explanation.walkthrough: The South African code comes from Dutch Zuid-Afrika; 'Sudden emphases' is the plural of the Italian musical term forzato.
explanation.definitionFit: Forzato, or sforzato, marks a note to be accented suddenly, and its plural names such sudden accents.

clue.text: Right at the back in Géricault masterpiece

parts.note: aft means at the back, toward a ship's stern

explanation.surface: A detail at the right, behind something, in a famous French painting.
explanation.walkthrough: Géricault's 'The Raft of the Medusa' (1819) is usually called simply 'The Raft'.
explanation.definitionFit: Géricault's most famous canvas shows the survivors of a shipwreck clinging to a makeshift vessel.

clue.text: King of humorists?

parts.note: reads as the best comic writer, but combines a Shakespearean king with the nonsense poet Edward of the same name

explanation.surface: Who is the greatest of all comic writers?
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's tragic King shares his name with Edward Lear, writer of nonsense verse and limericks, so he is both a king and a humorist.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to Shakespeare's king and to the Victorian nonsense poet.

clue.text: New US ray from sun-god

indicators.note: new tells the solver to make a fresh word from the letters of us ray

explanation.surface: A fresh American beam of light comes from a solar deity.
explanation.definitionFit: Surya is the Hindu deity of the sun.

clue.text: Possibly large part for 22

indicators.note: possibly allows the letters of large to be ordered another way

explanation.surface: Perhaps a big role for an actor playing the old king.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 across is Shakespeare's King Lear; a part fit for a king is kingly. The surface suggests his daughter Regan, a letter away.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingly bearing suits a monarch's role, so the adjective describes a part for the king.

clue.text: Like poem from taboo dictionary

indicators.note: from means the letters are drawn out of the words taboo dictionary

explanation.surface: Something resembling verse taken from a list of forbidden words.
explanation.definitionFit: Odic is the adjective from ode, a lyric poem, so it means relating to such a poem.

clue.text: Gulf history in The Yemen Diaries is only partly correct

indicators.note: in, backed by is only partly, shows the letters sit within the title The Yemen Diaries

explanation.surface: A Gulf history book is only partly accurate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is only partly' reads as a verdict on the book, but signals that only part of the title is used.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend a text is to correct it by removing errors.

clue.text: Paul Scott's still here, apparently

definitions.meaning: Paul Scott's 1977 Booker-winning novel about a British couple remaining in India after independence

explanation.surface: Paul Scott, it seems, has not left.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's novel title also means remaining in a place after the expected time to leave.

clue.text: Wild clerks I've sorted out, and one who married the marchioness down

indicators.note: sorted out tells the solver to put the letters of wild clerks I've into a new order

explanation.surface: Unruly office workers are dealt with, along with a man who wed a noblewoman.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop, the clerk Dick Swiveller marries the downtrodden servant girl he nicknames 'the Marchioness'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Dick Swiveller educates and later marries the servant he calls the Marchioness.
